lesson.title: How Much Does X Really Explain? The Coefficient of Determination
lesson.summary: R-squared measures the fraction of the total variation in y that the regression line accounts for, calculated by comparing leftover residual variation to total variation.
lesson.body:
The correlation coefficient r tells you the strength and direction of a linear relationship, but it does not directly answer a question people care about in practice: how much of the variation we see in y is actually explained by its relationship with x, versus how much is just unexplained scatter? That question is answered by the coefficient of determination, r-squared, which can be computed two equivalent ways: by squaring the correlation coefficient, or by directly comparing the leftover variation in the residuals to the total variation in y. Both methods are worth knowing, because the second one shows exactly why r-squared behaves the way it does, while the first is usually the faster calculation once r is already known.

The second method builds directly on residuals. Total variation in y is measured by the sum of squared deviations from the mean, SST = sum of (y minus y-bar) squared, which describes how spread out the y-values are before any regression line is even considered. Unexplained variation is measured by the sum of squared residuals, SSE = sum of (y minus y-hat) squared, which describes how spread out the y-values still are after accounting for the line. The coefficient of determination is r-squared = 1 - (SSE / SST), the proportion of total variation that is NOT left over as error, which is the same as saying the proportion that the regression line does explain.

Return to the study-hours data one more time: (1,55), (2,65), (3,70), (4,80), (5,88), mean y-bar = 71.6, fitted line y-hat = 47.3 + 8.1x. The residuals were -0.4, 1.5, -1.6, 0.3, 0.2, so SSE = 0.4-squared + 1.5-squared + 1.6-squared + 0.3-squared + 0.2-squared = 0.16 + 2.25 + 2.56 + 0.09 + 0.04 = 5.10. The total variation SST = sum of (y - 71.6)-squared over all five points = 275.56 + 43.56 + 2.56 + 70.56 + 268.96 = 661.2. So r-squared = 1 - (5.10 / 661.2) = 1 - 0.0077 = 0.9923.

That value, 0.9923, means about 99.2% of the variation in exam scores among these five students is explained by their linear relationship with hours studied, leaving only about 0.8% as unexplained scatter around the line. As a check, the correlation coefficient for this data works out to r = 0.996, and squaring it gives 0.996-squared = 0.992, matching the residual-based calculation (small differences are just rounding). Both routes to r-squared, squaring r or comparing SSE to SST, must always agree, because they are two derivations of the same quantity, and working a problem both ways is a good way to catch an arithmetic mistake in either the correlation or the residuals.

Notice how directly this depends on residuals: a model with tiny residuals produces a small SSE and therefore a large r-squared, while a model with large, scattered residuals produces a large SSE and a small r-squared. In that sense the coefficient of determination is really a residual plot compressed into a single number, a summary of how much leftover variation the line failed to explain, which sets up the next task of learning what that number does and does not mean in context. Because r-squared is always between 0 and 1 regardless of whether the relationship is positive or negative, it also loses the direction information that r carries, which is one reason both statistics are usually reported together rather than one in place of the other.
